title: Reforming the Judiciary -- Ch. 16: Estrada v. Sandiganbayan: The Anti-Plunder Law Is Constitutional
keywords: combination or series of overt or criminal acts
pattern of overt or criminal acts
primary_topics: Chapter 16 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- CJP's presentation of the Supreme Court's 10-4-1 ruling in Estrada v. Sandiganbayan upholding the constitutionality of the Anti-Plunder Law, framed by his own two-paragraph introduction and then carried by former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga's reprinted Kilosbayan article explaining the Decision and the Separate Opinions.

The origin and passage of Republic Act No. 7080 as recounted by its author Salonga -- filed in August 1988 out of the PCGG's experience with the Marcos cases, unanimously supported by the post-EDSA senators, and voted for repeatedly by Senator Estrada himself, who would later attack it as unconstitutional.

Justice Bellosillo's majority Decision holding that the law contains ascertainable standards and well-defined parameters, that 'combination' and 'series' carry their plain meanings as shown by the legislative deliberations, that Section 4's rule of evidence does not dispense with proof beyond reasonable doubt, and that Estrada, having voted for the law, cannot feign ignorance of it.

Justice Mendoza's concurrence that the doctrines of strict scrutiny, overbreadth and vagueness are analytical tools for free speech cases and inapt for penal statutes, so the Anti-Plunder Law must be tested only 'as applied' to Estrada, and that plunder is a malum in se requiring proof of mens rea.

Justice Panganiban's own Separate Concurring Opinion answering the dissenters point by point -- that the elements of plunder adequately answer the query 'What is the violation?', that the absence of statutory definitions is cured by judicial construction, that 'pattern' is procedural rather than an essential element, that RA 7080 is not patterned after the RICO Law, and that the quantum of evidence was not lowered.
sub_topics: CJP opens by recalling that on March 2, 2001, in Estrada v. Desierto and Estrada v. Arroyo, the Court unanimously upheld Gloria Macapagal Arroyo's ascension and ruled that Estrada had no immunity, since 'unlawful acts of public officials are not acts of the State.'

He explains that the Ombudsman then charged Estrada with plunder, a non-bailable crime under RA 7080, and that Estrada, 'in a bid to shortcut his detention and obtain immediate acquittal,' challenged the law's constitutionality; he states that he is reprinting, with permission, Salonga's Kilosbayan summary as this chapter.

Salonga begins with the announcement of the 10-4-1 vote on November 21, 2001, a day ahead of the scheduled promulgation, which he reads as the Court's move to stop the 'fearless forecasts' and text-message rumors smearing the justices.

He notes that Estrada's lawyers promised a motion for reconsideration before reading the majority opinion, while Senator Edgardo Angara called the move futile, and gives his own view that reversal is quite remote.

He recounts drafting the Anti-Plunder Act as Senate Bill No. 733 in August 1988, on the basis of his experience as first PCGG chair, pursuant to Executive Order No. 1's mandate of safeguards against ill-gotten wealth and the constitutional command to maintain honesty in public service.

He explains the need for the law: plunder or kleptocracy was unpunished, and malversation, falsification, theft, extortion and bribery were inadequate for the magnitude of Marcos-era corruption, which had forced some 80 separate complaints and endless delay; a single overall plunder charge would advance speedy justice for aggrieved and accused alike.

He rebuts Estrada's claim that it was a 'party bill' by naming the five coauthors he recruited across party lines and tracing the bill's progress -- Tanada's sponsorship on June 5, 1989, interpellations, second reading on June 6, third reading on July 25, 1989 by all nineteen senators present including Estrada, the bicameral reconciliation, approval of the Conference Committee Report on May 27, 1991, and President Aquino's approval on June 13, 1991.

He sets out the sequel: Estrada's election, his ouster by People Power II, Arroyo's oath before Chief Justice Davide on January 20, 2001, the four counts of plunder, the denial of his Motion to Quash on July 9, 2001, the 40-page Rule 65 petition, the absence of a TRO, and the Sandiganbayan's entry of a not-guilty plea when Estrada refused to plead.

He quotes the challenged provisions in full: Section 2 defining plunder at P50 million and its penalty of reclusion perpetua to death, Section 1(d)'s six categories of ill-gotten wealth, and Section 4's rule of evidence on proving a pattern.

He summarizes the Amended Information's four counts totaling more than four billion pesos: P545 million in illegal-gambling protection money, P130 million from the Ilocos Sur tobacco excise tax share, P189.7 million in commissions on GSIS and SSS purchases of Belle Corp. shares, and P3.23 billion deposited under the name 'Jose Velarde.'

He lists the three issues defined at the September 18, 2001 oral arguments -- vagueness, the claimed lowering of evidence for predicate crimes, and whether plunder is a malum prohibitum within Congress's power to so classify -- and names the counsel: Pacifico Agabin for Estrada, Solicitor-General Simeon Marcelo and Ombudsman Aniano Desierto for respondents.

He records the line-up: Bellosillo as ponente with nine concurring, separate concurrences by Mendoza and Panganiban, four dissents each with its own opinion by Kapunan, Pardo, Ynares-Santiago and Sandoval-Gutierrez, and Carpio abstaining as a former complainant.

Bellosillo's Decision, item by item: the presumption of constitutionality and Justice Malcolm's maxim 'To doubt is to sustain'; the ascertainable standards of Section 2; the plain meanings of 'combination' (two acts of different categories) and 'series' (two or more of the same); the common-understanding test for uncertainty; and Estrada's estoppel as a senator who voted for the bill 'with full knowledge of its legal implications.'

Bellosillo further holds that Section 4 does not dispense with proof beyond reasonable doubt but only relieves the prosecution of proving every one of many acts, that 'pattern' inheres in the acts of amassing wealth, and that the Death Penalty Law question was settled in People v. Echegaray.

Salonga quotes Bellosillo's peroration on the 'catastrophic looting of the national treasury,' plunder as a 'malignant tumor' and the law as 'a living testament to the will of the legislature,' closing with 'These are times that try men's souls.'

Mendoza's concurrence, item by item: the wholesale facial attack on provisions irrelevant to the Amended Information is improper; strict construction and strict scrutiny are different things, the former a rule of hermeneutics and the latter a standard of judicial review; deferential, intermediate and strict review are distinguished; and facial challenges for chilling effect belong to free speech cases, not penal statutes.

Mendoza also reads the congressional deliberations to fix 'combination,' 'series' and 'pattern,' explains Salonga's own illustration that proving ten of 150 acts suffices to show a pattern, calls the pattern 'the organizing principle' that welds discrete acts into one crime, and concludes that only problems of statutory construction remain.

Mendoza applies Connaly's vagueness test and Holmes's 'bad man' viewpoint from The Path of the Law, holds plunder a malum in se requiring mens rea because its constitutive crimes are inherently immoral and because Congress in 1993 listed it among heinous crimes, and rejects the disproportionate-penalty argument by analogy to other special complex crimes.

Panganiban's Separate Opinion on the first issue: citing Dans v. People and Sajul v. Sandiganbayan, a penal law is constitutional as long as it answers 'What is the violation?', and he enumerates the four elements of plunder that any law student could recite from the statute.

On the absence of definitions: 'simple statutory construction, not a declaration of unconstitutionality, is the key,' with the Bicameral Conference Committee of May 7, 1991 and the Senate deliberations of June 6, 1989 showing the shared understanding of combination and series, and Senator Neptali Gonzales's initial misgivings answered the very next day before he voted for the bill.

On further arguments: the law needs no minimum number of malefactors since plunder can be committed by a public officer acting alone, as even the RICO Law can be violated by one individual; items 4 and 5 of Section 1(d) do not criminalize innocent acts once read with Section 2, having antecedents in the Anti-Graft Law and the Revised Penal Code; and Estrada has not identified which protected freedom the law inhibits, so overbreadth fails.

On 'pattern': it is not an essential element but a rule of evidence, as Chief Justice Davide pointed out at oral argument that Section 2 deals with how plunder is committed and Section 4 with how it is proved, so Section 4 could be discarded without impairing the statute; and RA 7080 is not patterned after RICO, whose concern was long-term racketeering, whereas the Philippine law aimed at immediate deterrence of large-scale despoliation.

On the judicial power to construe: 'The power to declare what the law shall be is a legislative power. But the power to construe and apply the law is essentially judicial,' with the statute read in light of the evil to be suppressed -- the despoliation of the National Treasury by officials who held the levers of power -- and plunder as 'economic depredation which affects... the nation as a whole.'

On the second and third issues: the quantum of evidence was not lowered, since the indicative pattern must itself be proven beyond reasonable doubt in addition to the constitutive acts, making the burden greater than in an ordinary case; and whether plunder is classified as malum in se or prohibitum is not really significant, since the same burden of proof applies.

The article ends with the consequence: Estrada is now given the occasion to face the plunder charges on the merits and to show his innocence 'not by resorting to mere legalisms, but by showing the sheer falsity of the offenses attributed to him.'

notable_anecdotes: The early announcement: Salonga recounts that the Court announced its 10-4-1 vote on November 21, 2001, a day before the scheduled promulgation, to stop the 'fearless forecasts' and text messages smearing justices.

The author of the law on the accused: Salonga recalls that Estrada was a 6-month-old Liberal Party member when the Anti-Plunder Act was filed, was asked to oppose it if he wished, and instead voted for it not once but several times.
The 'party bill' answer: asked by media why he had voted for the law, Estrada called it a party bill -- which Salonga refutes by naming coauthors from three different parties.

The refused plea: when Estrada would not plead guilty or not guilty at his July 10, 2001 arraignment, the Sandiganbayan's 3rd Division under Justice Anacleto Badoy entered a plea of not guilty for him.

Davide at oral argument: Salonga records the Chief Justice pointing out from the bench that Section 2 deals with how plunder is committed and Section 4 with how it is proved -- the distinction Panganiban's opinion then turned on.
Carpio's abstention: Justice Antonio T. Carpio took no part because he had been one of the complainants against Estrada before the Ombudsman.
The smeared ponente: Salonga notes that Justice Bellosillo, who wrote the Decision, 'had been unjustly and ruthlessly smeared by zealous texters' before it came down.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 16 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' presented the Supreme Court's decision in Estrada v. Sandiganbayan upholding the Anti-Plunder Law. CJP supplied only the opening frame: he recalled that on March 2, 2001 the Court had unanimously upheld Gloria Macapagal Arroyo's ascension and denied Estrada immunity, that the Ombudsman then charged him with plunder under RA 7080, and that Estrada, 'in a bid to shortcut his detention and obtain immediate acquittal,' attacked the law's constitutionality; he then reprinted, with permission, former Senate President Jovito R. Salonga's Kilosbayan article as the chapter proper. Salonga, who had drafted the measure as Senate Bill No. 733 in August 1988 out of his PCGG experience, recounted its unanimous passage by the post-EDSA Senate -- including several affirmative votes by Senator Estrada himself -- and set out the charge of more than four billion pesos in illegal-gambling protection money, tobacco excise funds, Belle Corp. commissions and the 'Jose Velarde' deposits. He then explained the 10-4-1 Decision opinion by opinion. Justice Bellosillo held the law presumed constitutional, its standards ascertainable, its words 'combination' and 'series' plain on the legislative record, its Section 4 no dispensation from proof beyond reasonable doubt, and Estrada estopped from claiming ignorance of a law he had voted for. Justice Mendoza concurred that strict scrutiny, overbreadth and vagueness are tools for free speech cases and inapt for penal statutes, which must be judged as applied, and that plunder is a malum in se requiring mens rea. Justice Panganiban's own Separate Opinion answered the dissenters point by point: a penal law suffices if it answers 'What is the violation?'; 'simple statutory construction, not a declaration of unconstitutionality, is the key' to the undefined terms; 'pattern' is procedural rather than an essential element, so RA 7080 is not a copy of RICO; and the quantum of evidence was not lowered but raised. The article closed by noting that Estrada could now meet the charges on the merits, 'not by resorting to mere legalisms, but by showing the sheer falsity of the offenses attributed to him.'
